planting.note: Mount on a wood or cork slab, or grow in a wide, shallow basket of chunky orchid bark, since the broad shield fronds clasp whatever surface they're given rather than rooting into soil.

directions: This West African species produces broad, rounded, deeply veined shield fronds that overlap like shingles, plus undivided, strap-shaped fertile fronds that hang straight down instead of forking into antler tips as in most other staghorn ferns, which gives the plant its elephant-ear common name. Give it bright, indirect light and steady warmth above 60F, soaking the root mass thoroughly when the shield fronds begin to dry rather than watering on a fixed schedule. It is faster-growing and more shade-tolerant than many staghorns, making it a good choice for a bright bathroom or covered porch.

planting.note: Plant divisions in permanently moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered gully or streamside shade bed; this species has no tolerance for drying out.

directions: Native to the wet gullies and rainforest margins of southeastern Australia and Tasmania, hard water fern unfurls new fronds in a striking bronze-pink before maturing to stiff, leathery dark green, a color contrast that makes it stand out in a shaded fernery. Site it beside a stream, pond, or any permanently damp, shaded ground, since it struggles wherever soil dries between waterings. Bushwalkers in its native range sometimes call it leech fern, a nod to the boggy terrain it favors.

planting.note: Plant in permanently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil at a pond margin or shaded wetland edge; this species cannot tolerate drying out.

directions: Soft water fern forms loose clumps of pale, soft-textured fronds that emerge bright red before fading to light green, a gentler texture than the stiffer, darker hard water fern it often grows beside in southeastern Australian swamp forest. It tolerates genuinely waterlogged, poorly drained ground along creek banks and boggy hollows, conditions that would rot most other garden ferns, and spreads gradually by short creeping rhizomes. Give it full to dappled shade and keep the soil constantly damp for best results.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into crevices of a limestone wall, rock garden, or alpine trough in moist, sharply drained, calcium-rich soil, sited in shade or shelter from drying wind.

directions: First described from a sea cave near Aberdeen, Scotland, where it clings to dripping limestone walls in near-total darkness, Dickie's bladder fern is one of Europe's most specialized rock ferns and a lime-loving relative of the far more common brittle bladder fern. Its finely divided, grey-green fronds stay compact and spread slowly, making it better suited to a shaded crevice garden or alpine trough than an open border. The fronds can go summer-dormant in a dry spell but return reliably from the rhizome once moisture comes back.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or grow in a shallow basket of coarse, fast-draining epiphyte mix, letting the thick, scaly rhizomes creep freely over the container edge.

directions: Ranging from India through Taiwan, Malaysia, and the Pacific, rabbit's root fern produces long, thick, pale brown scaly rhizomes that scramble over bark, rock, or basket rim with a coarser, more vigorous habit than the smaller-rhizomed davallias already grown as houseplants. Mount it on a fern totem or slab and mist regularly, since the exposed creeping rhizome dries faster than the foliage despite handling brief dry spells better than most tropical epiphytes. Keep it warm and humid year-round in bright, indirect light, and let the mounting medium dry slightly between waterings to prevent rot.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in shaded limestone or sandstone rock crevices with humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil, mimicking the cliff ledges where it grows wild.

directions: This rare, naturally occurring hybrid between ebony spleenwort and walking fern was first found on a shaded sandstone ledge in Alabama, combining the glossy, near-black stipe of one parent with elongated, tapering frond tips that can root and form new plantlets where they touch soil, like the other parent. Most wild colonies are sterile, but a fertile population discovered in Vermont breeds true and supplies most plants in cultivation. Tuck it into a shaded rock crevice or tufa wall with constant, never soggy, moisture, and handle the narrow fronds gently since they are more brittle than either parent species.
